title: Deterministic Ceiling in Evaluating Verifier‑Augmented and LLM‑Only NetOps Agents
abstract: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. The design used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered identically to both conditions). Confirmatory outcomes reproduced exactly from archived analysis artifacts are: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400; guarded_success_count = 400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Execution and validator traces show repair_applied = false for all episodes and provider_call_audit records document hosted_model_call_event_count = 400 and stage_counts: {shared_initial_generation: 400}, empirically explaining a deterministic ceiling caused by identical per‑pair generation combined with a deterministic validator used for both runtime blocking and scoring. We present the preregistered methods, the exact artifact‑grounded results, diagnostics that identify the ceiling mechanism, and artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future runs so they meaningfully expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
LLM‑driven generation of network configuration artifacts promises to accelerate NetOps workflows, but safe end‑to‑end application demands that generated artifacts satisfy operational constraints (reachability, staged rollout safety, and rollback semantics). Prior work shows LLMs can synthesize plausible configuration templates and that verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. The central operational question addressed here is whether integrating a deterministic runtime validator into an LLM pipeline increases the empirical safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline when measured in a paired, action‑aware staging benchmark.

Research question and primary estimand. Under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1 semantics, does a verifier‑augmented agent yield a higher paired safe‑deploy rate than an LLM‑only agent? The preregistered primary estimand is the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 deterministic paired tasks using a paired‑binary confirmatory design and a permutation‑based test, with an exact McNemar test and paired bootstrap CIs prespecified for corroboration.

Scope and constraints. The experiment intentionally constrained generator calls (shared_initial_generation) and used a single deterministic validator both as a runtime guard and as the post‑hoc scorer. These choices were preregistered to isolate the validator’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs and to control model‑call accounting. As the archived execution shows, these choices produced a deterministic ceiling in this run; the manuscript reports the exact, artifact‑grounded outcome and explains why the design made the primary estimand uninformative for closed‑loop generator×guard dynamics.
sections.related_work: Three strands of verified literature motivate the design and interpretation. First, intent→configuration generation research establishes feasibility and identifies dataset and generalization gaps for LLMs applied to NetOps tasks (representative prototype and benchmark studies). These works demonstrate that LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration artifacts but tend to be evaluated on curated corpora or testbeds rather than in action‑aware staged deployment settings. Second, verifier‑guided workflows and deterministic verification in IaC and provisioning (including verifier‑in‑the‑loop architectures) show that strong verifiers can catch many errors offline and can guide repair or training (TerraFormer and related IaC work). Third, agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) broaden functional capability but introduce new failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tool use, and overconfidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Surveys and evaluation‑gap reviews repeatedly call for action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollout, repair, rollback, and provenance; our compact ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1 operationalizes these concerns and—through the completed run—exposes a concrete design pitfall for paired evaluations when generation variance and scorer determinism are conflated. The supplied evidence synthesis and cited records frame these findings and the hardening recommendations that follow.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory design. The study preregistration (cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1) specified a paired binary design with exactly N=400 paired tasks, primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, and a permutation‑based paired difference test as the primary confirmatory procedure. An exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs (percentile method) were prespecified for corroboration; bootstrap_seed = 1729 and bootstrap_resamples = 10,000 were recorded in archived analysis artifacts.

Execution contract and deterministic choices. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. The preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): for each task a single shared LLM candidate was generated and routed identically to both baseline and guarded episodes. This choice reduced model calls (model_calls_used = 400 for 800 episodes) and intentionally isolated acceptance decisions to the validator acting on identical candidates. The adapter permitted up to one repair call per guarded episode; repair_applied = false across all archived validator traces.

Task generation, replay, and scoring. Tasks were produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and include per‑task difficulty labels (level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}) and structured workflow constraints (required_sequence, expected_final_state). Deterministic three‑replay consistency checks were applied and passed for all pairs as required by the preregistration. Scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performing full intent‑constraint validation; validator traces record validation_before/after, normalized_configuration, required_command_count, valid flag, and repair_applied. These validator trace fields were inspected to diagnose the ceiling mechanism described below.

Statistical analysis. The registered executor 'paired_binary_analysis_v1' computed the paired contingency table and performed the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test and a permutation‑based paired difference test; bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were computed with the archived bootstrap_seed and resample count. All analysis code, seeds, and intermediate tables were archived and reproduced without manual adjudication.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (single shared generation per pair). Deterministic replay consistency checks passed for all pairs; exclusions = 0.

Confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). From the archived analysis outputs: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These numbers are reproduced verbatim from the archived confirmatory analysis artifacts.

Validator and provider diagnostics. Validator traces uniformly report valid = true in validation_before and validation_after and repair_applied = false for every episode; normalized_configuration and final_state fields in the validator traces match expected_final_state for accepted configurations. Provider and reconciliation artifacts show hosted_model_call_event_count = 400, cache_miss_count = 400, stage_counts: {shared_initial_generation: 400}, and condition_counts: {shared: 400}, empirically documenting the shared generation semantics and the absence of per‑condition generator variation. Together these records explain why both conditions recorded identical safe‑deploy outcomes for every pair: identical LLM outputs plus a deterministic validator that accepted those outputs forced concordant outcomes.

Difficulty aggregation and mitigation metrics. The archived task manifest yields the following difficulty distribution used in the run: medium: 80 tasks (20.0%); hard: 160 tasks (40.0%); very_hard: 160 tasks (40.0%). Across all 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; recorded mitigation metrics (repair attempts, repairs applied, time‑to‑rollback) are all zeros in the archived traces for this run.
sections.discussion:
Why a deterministic ceiling arose. Two preregistered operational choices produced the observed ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation eliminated generator variance by delivering the same LLM candidate to baseline and guarded episodes; provider_call_audit confirms 400 shared_initial_generation events and no per‑condition model calls beyond the shared candidate. Second, using the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) both as the runtime guard and as the post‑hoc scorer conflated runtime blocking and measurement. When the deterministic validator accepts a shared candidate, both conditions necessarily record safe‑deploy, so the paired difference is mechanically forced to zero. Validator traces demonstrating identical validation_before and validation_after fields and valid=true across episodes substantiate this mechanistic explanation.

Implications for confirmatory inference and preregistered power claims. The applied tests (permutation, exact McNemar, paired bootstrap) report p = 1.0 and a point mass CI at zero given the empirical data; these inferential outputs are numerically correct but scientifically uninformative about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics in this run because the preregistered design removed all opportunity for the guard to alter outcomes. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline failure rates; that assumption was falsified here by the frozen generator+validator pairing and therefore does not apply to the executed run.

Artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations. To preserve opportunities for runtime guards to accept, block, or request repair—and thereby restore inferential relevance for paired estimands—future preregistered designs should avoid conflating generator variance and scorer determinism. Concrete recommendations directly implementable using archived artifacts are:
1) Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition draws its own LLM candidate and the guard can act on distinct outputs. The execution manifest shows model_calls_used = 400 under shared semantics; switching to independent generation will increase model calls to at most 800 as permitted by the preregistration maximum.
2) Distinct post‑hoc scorer or held‑out adjudicator to avoid conflating runtime blocking and measurement (use a different validator implementation or a scorer with controlled stochastic perturbation). This prevents deterministic acceptances at runtime from guaranteeing identical scores.
3) Controlled adversarial seeding to guarantee nontrivial baseline failure rates (seed subsets of tasks that the generator is unlikely to satisfy without verifier intervention). The archived task manifest contains per‑task difficulty and required_sequence metadata enabling targeted adversarial selection.
4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling to ensure sufficient representation of very_hard tasks: the archived manifest already provides per‑task difficulty labels (medium:80; hard:160; very_hard:160) and supports deterministic stratified resampling for future runs.
5) Instrumented mitigation metrics (repair_attempts, repairs_applied, time‑to‑rollback) recorded as explicit numeric outcomes and included as secondary confirmatory measures. Validator traces in this run already record repair_applied and validation timestamps and can be extended to record repair attempt counts and timing in future executions.

Operational implications. Evaluations that reduce generator variance while scoring with the same deterministic verifier risk producing ceiling effects that mask verifier utility. Benchmarks intended to measure closed‑loop interactions should preserve independent sources of variability for generator and scorer and include adversarial or difficult tasks to exercise guard behaviors. The artifact archive produced here (task manifest, validator traces, provider call audit) supplies the necessary inputs to implement these hardening steps deterministically.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling is a design artifact caused by identical per‑pair generation and reuse of a deterministic validator for runtime blocking and post‑hoc scoring; it renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations (independent generation per condition, distinct scorer, controlled adversarial seeding, difficulty stratification, and mitigation metrics) give concrete steps to preserve statistical signal in future evaluations and can be implemented using the supplied task manifest and validator traces.

disclosure_statement: Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini. Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1. The immutable initial master prompt is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but none were applied (repair_applied = false). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle and were used without manual adjudication.
limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in the task manifest and can be aggregated by auditors; Table 1 reports the artifact‑extracted aggregated counts and percentages.
